1.problem: Arpon chooses a positive real number \(k\). For each positive integer \(n\), he places a marker at the point \((n,nk)\) in the \((x,y)\) plane. Suppose that two markers whose \(x\) coordinates differ by \(4\) have distance \(31\). What is the distance between the markers at \((7,7k)\) and \((19,19k)\)?
1.solutions: The difference of the \(x\)-coordinates of the markers is \(12=3\cdot4\). Thus, by similar triangles (where we draw right triangles whose legs are parallel to the axes and whose hypotenuses lie along the line \(y=kx\)), the distance between the markers is \(3\cdot31=93\).

2.problem: The real numbers \(x,y,z\) satisfy \(0\le x\le y\le z\le4\). If their squares form an arithmetic progression with common difference \(2\), determine the minimum possible value of \(|x-y|+|y-z|\).
2.solutions: Clearly, \[|x-y|+|y-z|=z-x=\frac{z^2-x^2}{z+x}=\frac4{z+x},\] which is minimized when \(z=4\) and \(x=\sqrt{12}\). Thus, our answer is \[4-\sqrt{12}=4-2\sqrt3.\]

3.problem: Find the rightmost non-zero digit of the expansion of \((20)(13!)\).
3.solutions: We can rewrite this as \[\begin{aligned} (20)(13!) &=(10\cdot2)(13\cdot12\cdot11\cdot10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1)\\ &=(10^3)(2\cdot13\cdot12\cdot11\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6\cdot4\cdot3). \end{aligned}\] Multiplying together the units digits for the terms not equal to \(10\) reveals that the rightmost non-zero digit is \(6\).

4.problem: Spencer is making burritos, each of which consists of one wrap and one filling. He has enough filling for up to four beef burritos and three chicken burritos. However, he only has five wraps for the burritos; in how many orders can he make exactly five burritos?
4.solutions: Spencer’s burrito-making can include either \(3\), \(2\), or \(1\) chicken burrito; consequently, he has \[\binom53+\binom52+\binom51=25\] orders in which he can make burritos.

5.problem: Rahul has ten cards face-down, which consist of five distinct pairs of matching cards. During each move of his game, Rahul chooses one card to turn face-up, looks at it, and then chooses another to turn face-up and looks at it. If the two face-up cards match, the game ends. If not, Rahul flips both cards face-down and keeps repeating this process. Initially, Rahul doesn’t know which cards are which. Assuming that he has perfect memory, find the smallest number of moves after which he can guarantee that the game has ended.
5.solutions:
Label the \(10\) cards \(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_5,b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_5\) such that \(a_i\) and \(b_i\) match for \(1\le i\le5\).

First, we’ll show that Rahul cannot always end the game in less than \(4\) moves. In particular, when he turns up his fifth card (during the third move), it is possible that the card he flips over is not one which he has yet encountered; consequently, he will not guarantee being able to match it, so he cannot guarantee that the game can end in three moves.

However, Rahul can always end the game in \(4\) moves. To do this, he can turn over \(6\) distinct cards in his first \(3\) moves. If we consider the \(5\) sets of cards \(\{a_1,b_1\},\{a_2,b_2\},\{a_3,b_3\},\{a_4,b_4\},\{a_5,b_5\}\), then by the pigeonhole principle, at least \(2\) of the \(6\) revealed cards must be from the same set. Rahul can then turn over those \(2\) cards on the fourth move, ending the game.

6.problem: Let \(R\) be the region in the Cartesian plane of points \((x,y)\) satisfying \(x\ge0\), \(y\ge0\), and \[x+y+\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor\le5.\] Determine the area of \(R\).
6.solutions:
We claim that a point in the first quadrant satisfies the desired property if the point is below the line \(x+y=3\) and does not satisfy the desired property if it is above the line.

For a point inside this region, \(x+y<3\) and \(\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor\le x+y<3\). However, \(\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor\) must be an integer. Thus, \(\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor\le2\). Adding these inequalities gives \[x+y+\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor<5,\] which satisfies the desired property. Conversely, for a point outside the region, \[\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor+\{x\}+\{y\}=x+y>3.\] But \(\{x\}+\{y\}<2\). Thus, \(\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor>1\), so \(\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor\ge2\), implying \[x+y+\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor>5.\]

To finish, \(R\) is the region bounded by the \(x\)-axis, the \(y\)-axis, and the line \(x+y=3\), a right triangle whose legs have length \(3\). Consequently, \(R\) has area \(\frac92\).

7.problem: Find the number of positive divisors \(d\) of \(15!=15\cdot14\cdots2\cdot1\) such that \(\gcd(d,60)=5\).
7.solutions: Since \(\gcd(d,60)=5\), we know that \(d=5^i d'\) for some integer \(i>0\) and some integer \(d'\) which is relatively prime to \(60\). Consequently, \(d'\) is a divisor of \(\frac{15!}{5^3}\); eliminating common factors with \(60\) gives that \(d'\) is a factor of \(7^2\cdot11\cdot13\), which has \[(2+1)(1+1)(1+1)=12\] factors. Finally, \(i\) can be \(1,2,\) or \(3\), so there are a total of \(3\cdot12=36\) possibilities.

8.problem: In a game, there are three indistinguishable boxes; one box contains two red balls, one contains two blue balls, and the last contains one ball of each color. To play, Raj first predicts whether he will draw two balls of the same color or two of different colors. Then, he picks a box, draws a ball at random, looks at the color, and replaces the ball in the same box. Finally, he repeats this; however, the boxes are not shuffled between draws, so he can determine whether he wants to draw again from the same box. Raj wins if he predicts correctly; if he plays optimally, what is the probability that he will win?
8.solutions:
Call the box with two red balls box 1, the box with one of each color box 2, and the box with two blue balls box 3. Without loss of generality, assume that the first ball that Bob draws is red. If Bob picked box 1, then he would have picked a red ball with probability \(1\), and if Bob picked box 2, then he would have picked a red ball with probability \(\frac12\). Therefore, the probability that he picked box 1 is \(\frac{1}{1+1/2}=\frac23\), and the probability that he picked box 2 is \(\frac13\). We will now consider both possible predictions and find which one gives a better probability of winning, assuming optimal play.

If Bob predicts that he will draw two balls of the same color, then there are two possible plays: he draws from the same box, or he draws from a different box. If he draws from the same box, then in the \(\frac23\) chance that he originally picked box 1, he will always win, and in the \(\frac13\) chance that he picked box 2, he will win with probability \(\frac12\), for a total probability of \[\frac23+\frac13\cdot\frac12=\frac56.\] If he draws from a different box, then if he originally picked box 1, he will win with probability \(\frac14\), and if he originally picked box 2, he will win with probability \(\frac12\), for a total probability of \[\frac23\cdot\frac14+\frac13\cdot\frac12=\frac13.\]

If Bob predicts that he will draw two balls of different colors, then we can consider the same two possible plays. Using similar calculations, if he draws from the same box, then he will win with probability \(\frac16\), and if he draws from a different box, then he will win with probability \(\frac23\). Looking at all cases, Bob’s best play is to predict that he will draw two balls of the same color and then draw the second ball from the same box, with a winning probability of \(\frac56\).

9.problem: I have \(8\) unit cubes of different colors, which I want to glue together into a \(2\times2\times2\) cube. How many distinct \(2\times2\times2\) cubes can I make? Rotations of the same cube are not considered distinct, but reflections are.
9.solutions: Our goal is to first pin down the cube, so it can’t rotate. Without loss of generality, suppose one of the unit cubes is purple, and let the purple cube be in the top left front position. Now, look at the three positions that share a face with the purple cube. There are \(\binom73\) ways to pick the three cubes that fill those positions and two ways to position them that are rotationally distinct. Now, we’ve taken care of any possible rotations, so there are simply \(4!\) ways to position the final four cubes. Thus, our answer is \[\binom73\cdot2\cdot4!=1680\] ways.

10.problem: Wesyu is a farmer, and she’s building a cao (a relative of the cow) pasture. She starts with a triangle \(A_0A_1A_2\) where angle \(A_0\) is \(90^\circ\), angle \(A_1\) is \(60^\circ\), and \(A_0A_1=1\). She then extends the pasture. First, she extends \(A_2A_0\) to \(A_3\) such that \(A_3A_0=\frac12A_2A_0\) and the new pasture is triangle \(A_1A_2A_3\). Next, she extends \(A_3A_1\) to \(A_4\) such that \(A_4A_1=\frac16A_3A_1\). She continues, each time extending \(A_nA_{n-2}\) to \(A_{n+1}\) such that \[A_{n+1}A_{n-2}=\frac1{2^n-2}A_nA_{n-2}.\] What is the smallest \(K\) such that her pasture never exceeds an area of \(K\)?
10.solutions:
For any \(i\), after performing the operation on triangle \(A_iA_{i+1}A_{i+2}\), the resulting pasture is triangle \(A_{i+1}A_{i+2}A_{i+3}\). Let \(K_i\) be the area of triangle \(A_iA_{i+1}A_{i+2}\). From \[A_{n+1}A_{n-2}=\frac1{2^n-2}A_nA_{n-2}\] and \[A_nA_{n+1}=A_nA_{n-2}+A_{n-2}A_{n+1},\] we have \[A_nA_{n+1}=\left(1+\frac1{2^n-2}\right)A_nA_{n-2}.\] We also know that the area of a triangle is half the product of its base and height. If we let the base of triangle \(A_{n-2}A_{n-1}A_n\) be \(A_nA_{n-2}\), its area is \(K_{n-2}=\frac12hA_nA_{n-2}\). The area of triangle \(A_{n-1}A_nA_{n+1}\) is \(K_{n-1}=\frac12hA_nA_{n+1}\). The heights are equal because the distance from \(A_{n-1}\) to the base does not change.

We now have \[\frac{K_{n-1}}{K_{n-2}}=\frac{A_nA_{n+1}}{A_nA_{n-2}}=1+\frac1{2^n-2}=\frac{2^n-1}{2^n-2}.\] Therefore, \[\frac{K_1}{K_0}=\frac32, \qquad \frac{K_2}{K_0}=\frac76\cdot\frac32=\frac74, \qquad \frac{K_3}{K_0}=\frac{15}{14}\cdot\frac74=\frac{15}{8}.\] We see the pattern \[\frac{K_n}{K_0}=\frac{2^{n+1}-1}{2^n},\] which can be easily proven by induction. As \(n\) approaches infinity, \(\frac{K_n}{K_0}\) grows arbitrarily close to \(2\), so the smallest \(K\) such that the pasture never exceeds an area of \(K\) is \(2K_0=\sqrt3\).

11.problem: Compute the prime factorization of \(1007021035035021007001\). (You should write your answer in the form \(p_1^{e_1}p_2^{e_2}\cdots p_k^{e_k}\), where \(p_1,\ldots,p_k\) are distinct prime numbers and \(e_1,\ldots,e_k\) are positive integers.)

12.problem: For how many integers \(1\le k\le2013\) does the decimal representation of \(k^k\) end with a \(1\)?
12.solutions: We claim that this is only possible if \(k\) has a units digit of \(1\). Clearly, it is true in these cases. Additionally, \(k^k\) cannot have a units digit of \(1\) when \(k\) has a units digit of \(2,4,5,6,\) or \(8\). If \(k\) has a units digit of \(3\) or \(7\), then \(k^k\) has a units digit of \(1\) if and only if \(4\mid k\), a contradiction. Similarly, if \(k\) has a units digit of \(9\), then \(k^k\) has a units digit of \(1\) if and only if \(2\mid k\), also a contradiction. Since there are \(202\) integers between \(1\) and \(2013\), inclusive, with a units digit of \(1\), there are \(202\) such \(k\) which fulfill our criterion.

13.problem: Find the smallest positive integer \(n\) such that \[\frac{5^{n+1}+2^{n+1}}{5^n+2^n}>4.99.\]
13.solutions: Writing \(5^{n+1}=5\cdot5^n\) and \(2^{n+1}=2\cdot2^n\) and cross-multiplying yields \[0.01\cdot5^n>2.99\cdot2^n.\] Rearranging gives \((2.5)^n>299\). A straightforward calculation shows that the smallest \(n\) for which this is true is \(n=7\).

14.problem: Consider triangle \(ABC\) with \(\angle A=2\angle B\). The angle bisectors from \(A\) and \(C\) intersect at \(D\), and the angle bisector from \(C\) intersects \(AB\) at \(E\). If \(\frac{DE}{DC}=\frac13\), compute \(\frac{AB}{AC}\).
14.solutions:
Let \(AE=x\) and \(BE=y\). Using the angle-bisector theorem on \(\triangle ACE\), we have \[x:DE=AC:DC,\] so \(AC=3x\). Angle chasing gives \(\angle ADE=\angle AED\), so \(AD=AE=x\).

Also, \(\triangle CDA\sim\triangle CEB\). Since \(DC:CE=3:4\), the similarity gives \(AD:BE=3:4\), so \(y=\frac43x\). Therefore \[AB=x+y=\frac73x, \qquad \frac{AB}{AC}=\frac{7x/3}{3x}=\frac79.\]

15.problem: Tim and Allen are playing a match of tenus. In a match of tenus, the two players play a series of games, each of which is won by one of the two players. The match ends when one player has won exactly two more games than the other player, at which point the player who has won more games wins the match. In odd-numbered games, Tim wins with probability \(3/4\), and in the even-numbered games, Allen wins with probability \(3/4\). What is the expected number of games in a match?
15.solutions: Let the answer be \(E\). If Tim wins the first game and Allen wins the second game, or vice versa, which occurs with probability \[\left(\frac34\right)^2+\left(\frac14\right)^2=\frac58,\] the expected number of additional games is \(E\), so the expected total number is \(E+2\). If one player wins both of the first two games, which has probability \(3/8\), there are exactly two games. It follows that \[E=\frac38\cdot2+\frac58(E+2),\] and solving gives \(E=\frac{16}{3}\).

16.problem: The walls of a room are in the shape of a triangle \(ABC\) with \(\angle ABC=90^\circ\), \(\angle BAC=60^\circ\), and \(AB=6\). Chong stands at the midpoint of \(BC\) and rolls a ball toward \(AB\). Suppose that the ball bounces off \(AB\), then \(AC\), then returns exactly to Chong. Find the length of the path of the ball.
16.solutions:
Let \(C'\) be the reflection of \(C\) across \(AB\), and let \(B'\) be the reflection of \(B\) across \(AC'\); angle chasing shows that \(B',A,C\) are collinear. The image of the path under these reflections is the line segment \(MM'\), where \(M\) is the midpoint of \(BC\) and \(M'\) is the midpoint of \(B'C'\). Thus the answer is the length of \(MM'\).

Applying the Law of Cosines to \(\triangle M'C'M\) gives \[MM'^2=27+243-2\cdot3\sqrt3\cdot9\sqrt3\cdot\frac12=189,\] so \(MM'=3\sqrt{21}\).

17.problem: The lines \(y=x\), \(y=2x\), and \(y=3x\) are the three medians of a triangle with perimeter \(1\). Find the length of the longest side of the triangle.
17.solutions:
The three medians of a triangle contain its vertices, so the vertices are \((a,a)\), \((b,2b)\), and \((c,3c)\) for some \(a,b,c\). The midpoint of \((a,a)\) and \((b,2b)\) lies on \(y=3x\), so \[\frac{a+2b}{2}=3\frac{a+b}{2},\] which gives \(b=-2a\). Similarly, the midpoint of \((b,2b)\) and \((c,3c)\) lies on \(y=x\), giving \(b=-2c\), so \(c=a\).

The vertices may therefore be written as \((a,a)\), \((-2a,-4a)\), and \((a,3a)\). Their side lengths are \[2|a|,\qquad \sqrt{34}|a|,\qquad \sqrt{58}|a|.\] Since the perimeter is \(1\), we have \(|a|=1/(2+\sqrt{34}+\sqrt{58})\), and the longest side has length \[\frac{\sqrt{58}}{2+\sqrt{34}+\sqrt{58}}.\]

18.problem: Define the sequence of positive integers \(\{a_n\}\) as follows. Let \(a_1=1\), \(a_2=3\), and for each \(n>2\), let \(a_n\) be the result of expressing \(a_{n-1}\) in base \(n-1\), then reading the resulting numeral in base \(n\), then adding \(2\) (in base \(n\)). For example, \(a_2=3_{10}=11_2\), so \(a_3=11_3+2_3=6_{10}\). Express \(a_{2013}\) in base ten.
18.solutions:
We claim that for nonnegative integers \(m\) and \(0\le n<3\cdot2^m\), \[a_{3\cdot2^m+n}=(3\cdot2^m+n)(m+2)+2n.\] We prove this by induction. The base case \(a_3=6\), when \(m=n=0\), is given in the problem.

Suppose the claim holds. If \(n<3\cdot2^m-1\), then writing \(a_{3\cdot2^m+n}\) in base \(3\cdot2^m+n\) gives the digits \(m+2\) and \(2n\). Reading these in the next base and adding \(2\) gives \[\begin{aligned} a_{3\cdot2^m+n+1} &=2+(3\cdot2^m+n+1)(m+2)+2n\\ &=(3\cdot2^m+n+1)(m+2)+2(n+1). \end{aligned}\] If \(n=3\cdot2^m-1\), the same computation gives \[\begin{aligned} a_{3\cdot2^{m+1}} &=2+(3\cdot2^{m+1})(m+2)+2(3\cdot2^m-1)\\ &=(3\cdot2^{m+1})((m+1)+2), \end{aligned}\] proving the next case as well.

Since \(2013=3\cdot2^9+477\), the formula gives \[a_{2013}=2013(9+2)+2(477)=23097.\]

19.problem: An isosceles trapezoid \(ABCD\) with bases \(AB\) and \(CD\) has \(AB=13\), \(CD=17\), and height \(3\). Let \(E\) be the intersection of \(AC\) and \(BD\). Circles \(\Omega\) and \(\omega\) are circumscribed about triangles \(ABE\) and \(CDE\). Compute the sum of the radii of \(\Omega\) and \(\omega\).
19.solutions:
Let \(\Omega\) have center \(O\) and radius \(R\), and let \(\omega\) have center \(P\) and radius \(M\). Let \(Q\) be the intersection of \(AB\) and \(OE\). The line \(OE\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\), and \(OE\) is a radius of \(\Omega\).

By similarity of \(\triangle AEB\) and \(\triangle CED\), the distance from \(E\) to \(AB\) is \[QE=\frac{13}{13+17}\cdot3=\frac{13}{10}.\] Also \(BQ=13/2\), so the Pythagorean theorem in \(\triangle OQB\) gives \[OQ=\sqrt{R^2-\left(\frac{13}{2}\right)^2}.\] Since \(OE=OQ+QE\), solving \[R=\frac{13}{10}+\sqrt{R^2-\left(\frac{13}{2}\right)^2}\] gives \(R=169/10\). By similarity, \(M=\frac{17}{13}R\), and therefore \[R+M=\frac{30}{13}R=39.\]

20.problem: The polynomial \(f(x)=x^3-3x^2-4x+4\) has three real roots \(r_1,r_2,\) and \(r_3\). Let \(g(x)=x^3+ax^2+bx+c\) be the polynomial which has roots \(s_1,s_2,\) and \(s_3\), where \[s_1=r_1+r_2z+r_3z^2, \quad s_2=r_1z+r_2z^2+r_3, \quad s_3=r_1z^2+r_2+r_3z,\] and \(z=\frac{-1+i\sqrt3}{2}\). Find the real part of the sum of the coefficients of \(g(x)\).
20.solutions:
Note that \(z=e^{2\pi i/3}\), so \(z^3=1\) and \(z^2+z+1=0\). Also \(s_2=s_1z\) and \(s_3=s_1z^2\). Thus the sum of the coefficients of \(g\) is \[g(1)=(1-s_1)(1-s_1z)(1-s_1z^2)=1-s_1^3.\]

Expanding, \[\begin{aligned} s_1^3={}&r_1^3+r_2^3+r_3^3 +3r_1^2r_2z+3r_1^2r_3z^2+3r_2^2r_3z+3r_2^2r_1z^2\\ &+3r_3^2r_1z+3r_3^2r_2z^2+6r_1r_2r_3. \end{aligned}\] The real parts of \(z\) and \(z^2\) are both \(-1/2\). By Vieta’s formulas, \[r_1+r_2+r_3=3,qquad r_1r_2+r_2r_3+r_3r_1=-4,qquad r_1r_2r_3=-4.\] Therefore \[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Re}(s_1^3) &=(r_1+r_2+r_3)^3-\frac92(r_1+r_2+r_3)(r_1r_2+r_2r_3+r_3r_1) +\frac{27}{2}r_1r_2r_3\\ &=27. \end{aligned}\] Hence \(\operatorname{Re}(g(1))=1-27=-26\).

21.problem: Find the number of positive integers \(j\le3^{2013}\) such that \[j=\sum_{k=0}^{m}(-1)^k\cdot3^{a_k}\] for some strictly increasing sequence of nonnegative integers \(\{a_k\}\). For example, we may write \(3=3^1\) and \(55=3^0-3^3+3^4\), but \(4\) cannot be written in this form.
21.solutions:
Clearly \(m\) must be even, or the sum would be negative. If \(a_m\le2013\), then the sum cannot exceed \(3^{2013}\), since \[j=3^{a_m}+\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(-1)^k3^{a_k}\le3^{a_m}.\] Likewise, if \(a_m>2013\), then the sum exceeds \(3^{2013}\), by the triangle inequality and a geometric-series estimate. Hence the elements of \(\{a_k\}\) may be any subset of \(\{0,1,\ldots,2013\}\) with an odd number of elements. Half of the \(2^{2014}\) subsets have odd size, giving \(2^{2013}\) possibilities.

It remains to show that different sequences give different values. Suppose two such sequences give the same value and choose a pair for which the larger of their maximum exponents is as small as possible. Since the leading power in an alternating sum exceeds the sum of all smaller possible powers, equality forces the two maximum exponents to be equal. Removing the common leading terms then gives two equal alternating sums with smaller maximum exponent, a contradiction. Thus every allowed sequence gives a distinct \(j\).

22.problem: Sherry and Val are playing a game. Sherry has a deck containing \(2011\) red cards and \(2012\) black cards, shuffled randomly. Sherry flips these cards over one at a time, and before she flips each card over, Val guesses whether it is red or black. If Val guesses correctly, she wins \(1\) dollar; otherwise, she loses \(1\) dollar. In addition, Val must guess red exactly \(2011\) times. If Val plays optimally, what is her expected profit from this game?
22.solutions:
We prove by induction on \(r+b\) that the expected profit when there are \(r\) red cards, \(b\) black cards, and \(g\) guesses which must be red is \[f(r,b,g)=(b-r)+\frac{2(r-b)}{r+b}g.\] The formula is readily checked in the one-card cases.

Assume it holds whenever the number of cards is less than \(r+b\). If Val guesses red, her expected profit is \[\frac{r}{r+b}\left(1+f(r-1,b,g-1)\right) +\frac{b}{r+b}\left(-1+f(r,b-1,g-1)\right),\] which simplifies to the stated formula. If she guesses black, her expected profit is \[\frac{r}{r+b}\left(-1+f(r-1,b,g)\right) +\frac{b}{r+b}\left(1+f(r,b-1,g)\right),\] which gives the same result. This proves the induction.

Substituting \((r,b,g)=(2011,2012,2011)\) gives \[1-\frac{2\cdot2011}{4023}=\frac{1}{4023}.\]

23.problem: Let \(ABCD\) be a parallelogram with \(AB=8\), \(AD=11\), and \(\angle BAD=60^\circ\). Let \(X\) be on segment \(CD\) with \(\frac{CX}{XD}=\frac13\) and \(Y\) be on segment \(AD\) with \(\frac{AY}{YD}=\frac12\). Let \(Z\) be on segment \(AB\) such that \(AX\), \(BY\), and \(DZ\) are concurrent. Determine the area of triangle \(XYZ\).
23.solutions: Let \(AX\) and \(BD\) meet at \(P\). We have \[\frac{DP}{PB}=\frac{DX}{AB}=\frac34.\] Applying Ceva’s Theorem in \(\triangle ABD\) gives \[\frac{AZ}{ZB}=\frac{DP}{PB}\cdot\frac{AY}{YD}=\frac34\cdot\frac12=\frac38.\] Now \[\frac{[AYZ]}{[ABCD]}=\frac12\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac3{11}=\frac1{22}, \qquad \frac{[DYX]}{[ABCD]}=\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac34=\frac14.\] Also, \[\frac{[XCBZ]}{[ABCD]}=\frac12\left(\frac14+\frac8{11}\right)=\frac{43}{88}.\] Thus \(\triangle XYZ\) occupies \[1-\frac1{22}-\frac14-\frac{43}{88}=\frac{19}{88}\] of the parallelogram. Therefore its area is \[8\cdot11\cdot\sin60^\circ\cdot\frac{19}{88}=\frac{19\sqrt3}{2}.\]

24.problem: Given a point \(p\) and a line segment \(l\), let \(d(p,l)\) be the distance between them. Let \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) be points in the plane such that \(AB=6\), \(BC=8\), \(AC=10\). What is the area of the region in the \((x,y)\)-plane formed by the ordered pairs \((x,y)\) such that there exists a point \(P\) inside triangle \(ABC\) with \[d(P,AB)+x=d(P,BC)+y=d(P,AC)?\]
24.solutions:
Place \(ABC\) in the coordinate plane so that \(A=(0,6)\), \(B=(0,0)\), and \(C=(8,0)\). Let \(P=(a,b)\) be inside \(\triangle ABC\). Then \(d(P,AB)=a\) and \(d(P,BC)=b\).

The area of \(\triangle ABC\) is \(24\), and it is also the sum of the areas of \(\triangle PAB\), \(\triangle PBC\), and \(\triangle PCA\). The first two areas are \(3a\) and \(4b\), respectively, so \[d(P,CA)=\frac{24-3a-4b}{5}.\] It follows that \[(x,y)=\left(\frac{24-8a-4b}{5},\frac{24-3a-9b}{5}\right).\]

The allowed \((a,b)\) satisfy \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge0\), and \(6a+8b\le48\). Since the displayed map is affine, its image is the triangle obtained from the three vertices \((0,0)\), \((0,6)\), and \((8,0)\). Their images are \[\left(\frac{24}{5},\frac{24}{5}\right),qquad (0,-6),qquad (-8,0).\] The area of the triangle with these vertices is, by a determinant computation, \[\frac{288}{5}.\]

25.problem:
The sequence \((z_n)\) of complex numbers satisfies the following properties:

  • \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) are not real.
  • \(z_{n+2}=z_{n+1}^2z_n\) for all integers \(n\ge1\).
  • \(\frac{z_{n+3}}{z_n^2}\) is real for all integers \(n\ge1\).
  • \(\left|\frac{z_3}{z_4}\right|=\left|\frac{z_4}{z_5}\right|=2\).

Find the product of all possible values of \(z_1\).
25.solutions:
Write \(z_n=r_ne^{i\theta_n}\). From the recurrence, \[\frac{z_{n+3}}{z_n^2} =\frac{z_{n+2}^2z_{n+1}}{z_n^2} =z_{n+1}^5.\] This is real for all \(n\ge1\), so \(\theta_n=\pi k_n/5\) for all \(n\ge2\), where each \(k_n\) is an integer. Since \(\theta_1+2\theta_2=\theta_3\), we may also write \(\theta_1=\pi k_1/5\).

For the magnitudes, the given ratios and the recurrence give \[\frac{r_3}{r_4}=\frac{r_4}{r_5}=2, \qquad r_5=r_4^2r_3,\] so \(r_3=1\). Then \(r_4=1/2\), \(r_4=r_3^2r_2\) gives \(r_2=1/2\), and \(r_3=r_2^2r_1\) gives \(r_1=4\).

Thus the possible values of \(z_1\) are the nonreal roots of \(x^{10}-4^{10}=0\). There are eight such roots. The product of all ten roots is \(-4^{10}\), while the product of the two real roots \(4\) and \(-4\) is \(-4^2\). Hence the desired product is \[\frac{4^{10}}{4^2}=4^8=65536.\] For each of these values, a valid sequence can be constructed by choosing a nonreal \(z_2\) with \(|z_2|=1/2\) and suitable argument.

26.problem: Triangle \(ABC\) has perimeter \(1\). Its three altitudes form the side lengths of a triangle. Find the set of all possible values of \(\min(AB,BC,CA)\).
26.solutions:
Let \(a,b,c\) denote the side lengths \(BC,CA,AB\), respectively. Without loss of generality assume \(a\le b\le c\); we seek the range of \(a\). The largest possible value is \(1/3\), attained by an equilateral triangle.

Write \(c=xa\) and \(b=ya\), where \(x\ge y\ge1\). For a nonequilateral triangle, \(x>1\). The triangle inequality \(a+b>c\) gives \[y>x-1.\] If \(K\) is the area, the altitudes are \(2K/a,2K/b,2K/c\). Their triangle inequality gives \[\frac{2K}{c}+\frac{2K}{b}>\frac{2K}{a},\] or \(y<x/(x-1)\). Therefore \[x-1<\frac{x}{x-1},\] which gives \(x<(3+\sqrt5)/2\).

Since \(a(1+x+y)=1\), a lower bound for \(a\) comes from an upper bound for \(1+x+y\). We have \[1+x+y<1+x+\frac{x}{x-1}=x+\frac{1}{x-1}+2.\] On the allowed interval this is less than \(3+\sqrt5\), so \[a>\frac{1}{3+\sqrt5}=\frac{3-\sqrt5}{4}.\] The endpoint is not attained. Conversely, for every \(a\) in this interval one may choose suitable \(b,c\) (using \(b=c=(1-a)/2\) for part of the range, and the construction in the inequalities above for the rest), and the triangle and altitude inequalities hold. Thus the set is \[\left(\frac{3-\sqrt5}{4},\frac13\right].\]

27.problem: Let \(W\) be the hypercube \[\{(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)\mid0\le x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\le1\}.\] The intersection of \(W\) and a hyperplane parallel to \(x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=0\) is a non-degenerate \(3\)-dimensional polyhedron. What is the maximum number of faces of this polyhedron?
27.solutions: The number of faces of the polyhedron equals the number of distinct \(3\)-dimensional faces of the hypercube whose interiors the hyperplane intersects, so it is at most \(8\). This bound is attained: the hyperplane \[x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=\frac32\] intersects all eight faces. For example, it passes through \((0,\frac12,\frac12,\frac12)\) on \(x_1=0\) and \((1,\frac16,\frac16,\frac16)\) on \(x_1=1\); permuting coordinates gives interior points on the other six faces. Thus the maximum is \(8\).

28.problem: Let \(z_0+z_1+z_2+\cdots\) be an infinite complex geometric series such that \(z_0=1\) and \[z_{2013}=\frac{1}{2013^{2013}}.\] Find the sum of all possible sums of this series.
28.solutions: The possible common ratios are the \(2013\) roots \(r_1,\ldots,r_{2013}\) of \[r^{2013}=\frac{1}{2013^{2013}}.\] The corresponding sums are \(x_n=1/(1-r_n)\). Since \[\left(1-\frac1{x_n}\right)^{2013}=\frac{1}{2013^{2013}},\] the \(x_n\) are the roots of \[2013^{2013}(x-1)^{2013}-x^{2013}=0.\] The leading coefficient is \(2013^{2013}-1\), and the coefficient of \(x^{2012}\) is \(-2013^{2014}\). By Vieta’s formulas, the sum of the roots is \[\frac{2013^{2014}}{2013^{2013}-1}.\]

29.problem: Let \(A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_m\) be finite sets of size \(2012\) and let \(B_1,B_2,\ldots,B_m\) be finite sets of size \(2013\) such that \(A_i\cap B_j=\varnothing\) if and only if \(i=j\). Find the maximum value of \(m\).
29.solutions:
More generally, suppose each \(A_i\) has \(a\) elements and each \(B_i\) has \(b\) elements. We show that the maximum value of \(m\) is \(\binom{a+b}{a}\).

Let \(U\) be the union of all the sets and let \(|U|=n\). Consider all \(n!\) orderings of the elements of \(U\). For any particular ordering, there is at most one \(i\) for which every element of \(A_i\) comes before every element of \(B_i\). Indeed, for \(j\ne i\), \(A_j\) shares an element with \(B_i\), and \(B_j\) shares an element with \(A_i\).

For a fixed \(i\), the number of permutations of the \(a+b\) elements of \(A_i\cup B_i\) in which all elements of \(A_i\) come first is \(a!b!\). Hence the number of orderings of \(U\) with this property is \[n!\frac{a!b!}{(a+b)!}=\frac{n!}{\binom{a+b}{a}}.\] Summing over \(i\) and using the fact that at most \(n!\) orderings are counted gives \[m\frac{n!}{\binom{a+b}{a}}\le n!,\] so \(m\le\binom{a+b}{a}\).

Equality is attained by taking \(U\) to have \(a+b\) elements, letting the \(A_i\) range over all \(a\)-element subsets of \(U\), and setting \(B_i=U\setminus A_i\). With \(a=2012\) and \(b=2013\), the answer is \(\binom{4025}{2012}\).

30.problem: How many positive integers \(k\) are there such that \[\frac{k}{2013}(a+b)=\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\] has a solution in positive integers \((a,b)\)?
30.solutions:
Let \(h=\gcd(a,b)\) and write \((a,b)=(hA,hB)\) with \(\gcd(A,B)=1\). Substitution gives \[k=\frac{2013AB}{A+B}.\] Since \(A+B\) is relatively prime to both \(A\) and \(B\), \(k\) is an integer exactly when \(A+B\) divides \(2013\); also \(A+B>1\).

Different values of \(A+B\) give different \(k\). Indeed, if \[\frac{2013AB}{A+B}=\frac{2013A'B'}{A'+B'},\] then coprimality shows that \(A+B\) divides \(A'+B'\) and conversely, so the sums are equal.

For a fixed sum \(n=A+B=C+D\), equality of the corresponding values of \(k\) gives \(A(n-A)=C(n-C)\), so \((C-A)(C+A-n)=0\). Hence \((C,D)\) is a permutation of \((A,B)\). Therefore, for each divisor \(n>1\) of \(2013\), there are \(\varphi(n)/2\) distinct values. Using \(\sum_{d\mid2013}\varphi(d)=2013\), the total is \[\frac{2013-1}{2}=1006.\]

31.problem: Let \(ABCD\) be a quadrilateral inscribed in a unit circle with center \(O\). Suppose that \(\angle AOB=\angle COD=135^\circ\), \(BC=1\). Let \(B'\) and \(C'\) be the reflections of \(A\) across \(BO\) and \(CO\) respectively. Let \(H_1\) and \(H_2\) be the orthocenters of \(AB'C'\) and \(BCD\), respectively. If \(M\) is the midpoint of \(OH_1\), and \(O'\) is the reflection of \(O\) about the midpoint of \(MH_2\), compute \(OO'\).
31.solutions: Place the diagram on the complex plane with \(O\) at the origin and \(A\) at \(1\). Let \(B\) have coordinate \(b\) and \(C\) have coordinate \(c\). Then \(B'\) has coordinate \(b^2\), \(C'\) has coordinate \(c^2\), and \(D\) has coordinate \(bc\). Since the orthocenter of a triangle inscribed in the unit circle is the sum of its vertices, \[H_1=1+b^2+c^2, \qquad H_2=b+c+bc.\] Thus \(M=\frac12(1+b^2+c^2)\), and reflecting \(O\) about the midpoint of \(MH_2\) gives \[O'=\frac12(1+b^2+c^2+2b+2c+2bc)=\frac12(b+c+1)^2.\] Hence \(OO'=\frac12|b+c+1|^2\). We have \(b=\operatorname{cis}135^\circ\) and \(c=\operatorname{cis}195^\circ\), and substitution gives \[OO'=\frac14(8-\sqrt6-\sqrt2).\]

32.problem:
For an even positive integer \(n\) Kevin has a tape of length \(4n\) with marks at \(-2n,-2n+1,\ldots,2n-1,2n\). He then randomly picks \(n\) points in the set \(-n,-n+1,-n+2,\ldots,n-1,n\), and places a stone on each of these points. We call a stone ‘stuck’ if it is on \(2n\) or \(-2n\), or either all the points to the right, or all the points to the left, all contain stones. Then, every minute, Kevin shifts the unstuck stones in the following manner:

  • He picks an unstuck stone uniformly at random and then flips a fair coin.
  • If the coin came up heads, he then moves that stone and every stone in the largest contiguous set containing that stone one point to the left. If the coin came up tails, he moves every stone in that set one point right instead.
  • He repeats until all the stones are stuck.

Let \(p_k\) be the probability that at the end of the process there are exactly \(k\) stones in the right half. Evaluate \[\frac{p_{n-1}-p_{n-2}+p_{n-3}-\cdots+p_3-p_2+p_1} {p_{n-1}+p_{n-2}+p_{n-3}+\cdots+p_3+p_2+p_1}\] in terms of \(n\).
32.solutions:
After selecting the initial positions, number them \(a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_n\). The movement rules imply that the expected value of \(a_i-a_j\) remains unchanged after each minute. If \(b_i\) is the final position of the \(i\)th stone, then \[E(b_{i+1}-b_i)=E(a_{i+1}-a_i).\] If the final configuration has exactly \(i\) stones on one side and \(n-i\) on the other, this gap is \(3n+2\); otherwise it is \(1\). Hence \[E(b_{i+1}-b_i)=(3n+2)p_i+1(1-p_i).\]

By symmetry of the uniformly chosen initial \(n\)-subset of the \(2n+1\) available positions, the expected gaps \(E(a_{i+1}-a_i)\) are independent of \(i\). Therefore \(p_i\) is constant for \(1\le i\le n-1\). Since \(n\) is even, the numerator is one copy of this common value and the denominator is \(n-1\) copies, so the requested ratio is \[\frac{1}{n-1}.\]
